## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="t12-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Dominated plan</dt><dd>Another plan costs no more and emits no more, and is better on one count: nobody should pick it.</dd>
<dt>Weighted sum</dt><dd>Score each plan by cost plus a carbon price times its CO₂; the lowest score wins.</dd>
<dt>Epsilon-constraint</dt><dd>Cap the CO₂ and find the cheapest plan under the cap; sweep the cap to trace the frontier.</dd>
<dt>Frontier</dt><dd>The plans that cannot get cheaper without getting dirtier, or cleaner without getting dearer.</dd>
<dt>Shadow price</dt><dd>Used as a carbon price, the cap's shadow price makes the cap's plan one of the cheapest choices.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The limits of weighted sums</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li><b>Dents.</b> Plan C ($131.4M, 488 kt) lies above the straight line from B to D, so no carbon price picks it, though no plan beats it on both counts. Frontiers built from yes-or-no choices, such as building a plant or not, often have such dents.</li>
<li><b>Nearly straight pieces.</b> Between 500 and 400 kt the slope barely changes ($43.4 to $44.0 a tonne), so prices from $43 to $45 move the plan from 541 kt to 389 kt.</li>
<li><b>Uneven spacing.</b> Even steps in price give uneven steps along the frontier: up to $45 a tonne moves the plan from 792 kt to below 400 kt; from $45 to $220 it moves only to 100 kt.</li>
<li><b>Weights carry units.</b> The weight in cost + <i>w</i> × CO₂ is a price in dollars per tonne; measure CO₂ in kilotonnes and the same number means something a thousand times larger.</li>
</ul>
<p>Das and Dennis (1997) showed these drawbacks for weighted sums in general. The epsilon-constraint method avoids the first two by fixing one goal and optimizing the other.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The cap's dual as a carbon price</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

The [epsilon-constraint]{.lx-term term="epsilon-constraint"} problem: the cheapest plan under a CO₂ cap.

$$\min_x \; c(x) \quad \text{subject to} \quad e(x) \le \varepsilon \;\; (\lambda), \;\; x \in X.$$

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| $x$, $X$ | a plan (what to build and how to run it), and every plan that meets the other rules |
| $c(x)$, $e(x)$ | its yearly cost (\$) and its CO₂ (tonnes) |
| $\varepsilon$ | the cap, in tonnes a year |
| $\lambda$ | the cap's multiplier, or dual: its shadow price, in \$ per tonne |
| $\lambda^*$, $c^*(\varepsilon)$ | that multiplier at the best plan, and the best cost for cap $\varepsilon$ |

- **Duality.** For a linear program, strong duality (a theorem that pairs every LP with a "dual" LP of prices) guarantees a $\lambda^* \ge 0$ for which the cap's best plan also minimizes the [weighted sum]{.lx-term term="weighted-sum"} $c(x) + \lambda^* e(x)$. Other plans may tie with it, and a solver may return one of them.
- **Slope.** Where the frontier is smooth, $\lambda^* = -\,\mathrm{d}c^*/\mathrm{d}\varepsilon$; at a kink, $\lambda^*$ lies between the slopes on either side.
- **Here.** A 200 kt cap has $\lambda^* = \$85.2$ per tonne; a \$85.2 price with no cap lands at 199 kt and \$129.3M.
- **Ties.** On an exactly straight piece every plan ties at its slope; with integer decisions there is no such guarantee at all.

Mavrotas (2009) shows how to sweep $\varepsilon$ efficiently. Upcoming: M6 (carbon in models) and A22 (five goals at once).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="t12-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cheapest" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The cheapest plan is always the right choice.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Here plan A stays the pick only while CO₂ is priced below $53 a tonne. The frontier shows what each tonne avoided costs; people decide what that is worth.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="same" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A carbon price and a CO₂ cap can lead to the same plan.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. A 200 kt cap has a shadow price of $85.2 a tonne; that price, with no cap, lands at 199 kt, next to the cap's plan.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="every" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every plan that is not dominated can be picked by some carbon price.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Plan C is not dominated, yet it sits in a dent between B and D, so no price picks it.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="t12">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="switch" data-answer="a">
<p class="lx-qtext">Plan B costs $119.4M a year and emits 521 kt; plan D costs $136.8M and emits 249 kt. Above what carbon price does D score lower than B?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">About $64 a tonne</li><li data-value="b">About $17 a tonne</li><li data-value="c">About $273 a tonne</li><li data-value="d">D never scores lower</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>About $64: D costs $17.4M more and emits 272 kt less, and 17.4 million ÷ 272,000 tonnes ≈ $64 a tonne.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
